Ten minutes before the inter-school music round, with the hall already filling, Bhavna grabbed her friend Rekha's arm backstage. "Tell me honestly. Am I okay?"
Rekha prided herself on never sugar-coating. "Honestly? You go flat on the high notes. You'll probably embarrass yourself." She said it quickly, almost pleased with how clear it sounded.
There was no time to practise, nothing Bhavna could fix. Her face went pale. On stage she started too quietly and never recovered.
Afterwards Rekha told the others, "Someone had to be real with her." But on the bus home she remembered the small satisfied feeling she'd had while saying it, and it didn't feel like honesty any more. It felt more like winning.

qa.q: When did Bhavna ask Rekha for an honest opinion?
qa.a: Ten minutes before the inter-school music round, backstage.

qa.q: What did Rekha realise on the bus home?
qa.a: She realised her comment had come with a small satisfied feeling, so it felt more like winning than honesty.

qa.q: What could Rekha have said ten minutes before the round?
qa.a: With no time to fix anything, she could have offered encouragement, like reminding Bhavna to breathe, and saved honest notes for later when they could help.

qa.q: How did Rekha's words affect Bhavna on stage?
qa.a: They shook her confidence; she went pale, started too quietly and never recovered.

grounding: A teenage girl who prides herself on bluntness tells her friend her singing is bad at the worst moment, and later senses it served her own need to feel superior.

In her Kolkata flat, Gurleen scrolled to Tanuja's new video: her friend singing an old film song on the balcony, eyes closed. Gurleen typed a comment: "Brutal honesty, since no one else will say it: this is really off-key. Real friends tell the truth."
Within an hour it had twenty likes. Gurleen kept refreshing, enjoying each one. She told herself she was the only real one in the group.
By evening the video was gone. Tanuja's status just said "lesson learned". At tuition the next day she sat at the far end and didn't look up.
When Gurleen's cousin saw the comment, she asked quietly, "If it was for Tanuja, why say it where everyone could see?" Gurleen didn't answer. She still didn't have an answer.

qa.q: How many likes did Gurleen's comment get within an hour?
qa.a: It had twenty likes within an hour.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen keep refreshing the comment?
qa.a: She enjoyed the likes and felt like the only real one in the group, which suggests the comment served her need to feel superior.

qa.q: What could Gurleen do now?
qa.a: She could delete the comment, apologise to Tanuja privately, and offer kind, specific feedback only if Tanuja wants it.

qa.q: What is it like for Tanuja after the comment?
qa.a: She feels humiliated and hurt; she deleted the video, wrote "lesson learned" and sat at the far end without looking up.

grounding: A teenage girl posts 'brutal honesty' about her friend's singing where everyone can see, and the bluntness serves her image more than the friend's growth.

After music club, Dilnaz packed up her notebook of songs while the others stacked the chairs.
"You want the truth?" Santosh said, leaning against the harmonium. "You were flat on every high note. Honestly, singing isn't your thing."
Dilnaz froze. Two girls near the door went quiet.
"I'm just being honest," Santosh added, loudly enough for them to hear. "Everyone else here is too scared to tell you."
Dilnaz left without a word. Santosh felt sharp and clever for a second, like the only brave person in the room.
The music teacher, who had heard, called him over. "Was that for her, or for you?"
"For her. She needs to know."
"Then why did you say it in front of everyone? And why didn't you mention how much better her breathing has got since June?"
Santosh opened his mouth, then shut it. He didn't have an answer he liked.

qa.q: What did Santosh say about Dilnaz's high notes?
qa.a: He said she was flat on every high note.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel right after Dilnaz left?
qa.a: Santosh felt sharp and clever, even proud, like the only brave person in the room, which showed the bluntness served him.

qa.q: What could Santosh have done if he really wanted to help Dilnaz?
qa.a: He could have spoken to her privately, mentioned what had improved, like her breathing, and offered one specific thing to work on.

qa.q: What was it like for Dilnaz to hear this in front of others?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt humiliated and hurt, freezing and leaving without a word, because the criticism came publicly and with no kindness.

grounding: It shows a teenager proud of blunt honesty calling a friend's singing bad in public, when the bluntness served his wish to feel superior.

passage:
Subject: about yesterday

Hi Seema,
Yesterday after the talent show, I told you your singing was bad and that you should stop entering competitions. I said it was "just the truth." You went quiet the whole way home.
I've been thinking about why I said it like that. Part of me thought it was honest. But if I'm honest now, it felt good to say. Like I knew better. Like I was above everyone clapping. You looked so hurt, and I kept talking.
The truth is smaller than what I said. Your low notes are really beautiful. You rushed the second verse because you were nervous. That's it. That's all I actually noticed.
I'm sorry I made it sound like you should give up. I don't think that at all.
Can I come to your practice on Saturday? I'll bring samosas and keep my opinions to the useful ones.
Trisha

qa.q: What did Trisha say Seema rushed?
qa.a: Seema rushed the second verse because Seema was nervous.

qa.q: What does Trisha admit about how saying it felt?
qa.a: Trisha admits it felt good and superior to say it, like Trisha knew better than everyone clapping, which now makes Trisha feel guilty.

qa.q: What does Trisha do to repair things?
qa.a: Trisha apologises, gives the smaller true feedback kindly, and offers to come to Seema's practice on Saturday.

qa.q: How did Seema feel after the talent show?
qa.a: Seema felt hurt and crushed, going quiet the whole way home after being told to stop entering competitions.

grounding: A teenager's email to a friend admits that brutal honesty about the friend's singing served the writer's own feeling of superiority.

Darshan, you won't believe what happened at the choir audition. So Pallavi sings, right? And after, she comes up to me and asks, "How was it?" And I said, "Honestly? Bad. You were off-key the whole time." Because I'm Keerthana. I don't do fake. Everyone knows that about me.
And she just… looked at me. And then walked away. Now her friends aren't talking to me. For being honest!
Why are you making that face?
…Okay, fine, I didn't have to say "bad." And maybe I didn't have to say it right there in the corridor. And maybe it felt a bit good to be the one who knows. Like I'm above all those people who just say "nice."
But she was off-key.
Darshan, stop looking at me like that. What would you have said?
…"You were nervous, the first line was really strong, want to practise together?" Ugh. Yeah. That's better.

qa.q: Where did Keerthana give Pallavi her opinion?
qa.a: Right there in the corridor.

qa.q: What does Keerthana admit about how saying it felt?
qa.a: Keerthana admits it felt a bit good and superior, like being above people who just say "nice," which starts to make Keerthana uneasy.

qa.q: What better response does Keerthana reach by the end?
qa.a: Keerthana reaches a kinder, honest version: noting Pallavi was nervous, praising the strong first line and offering to practise together.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt when Keerthana said "Bad"?
qa.a: Pallavi probably felt hurt and embarrassed, which is why she looked at Keerthana and walked away.

grounding: A teenager proud of bluntness tells a friend her singing was bad and slowly sees that it served her need to feel superior.

Monday: After choir practice, Lakshmi asked Sunaina how her solo had sounded. "Honestly? Flat. Really flat. Someone had to tell you," Sunaina said, and felt clever saying it. She always said she was the only honest one.
Thursday: Lakshmi's name was missing from the choir list for annual day. She had dropped out. At lunch she sat with other girls and didn't look at Sunaina.
The next Wednesday: In music class, Sunaina heard their teacher tell Lakshmi, "Your high notes are lovely. Let's work on breath for the low ones." Lakshmi smiled for the first time in days. Sunaina's cheeks burned. The teacher had said something true too, but it had helped. Hers had only made her feel bigger.
That evening she messaged Lakshmi: "I was mean, not honest. Your high notes ARE nice. Sorry." Lakshmi replied an hour later: "Thanks. That actually helps."

qa.q: What did Sunaina say about Lakshmi's solo?
qa.a: 'Honestly? Flat. Really flat.'

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel when saying the solo was flat?
qa.a: Sunaina felt clever and superior, proud of being 'the only honest one'.

qa.q: What did the teacher's feedback show that Sunaina's didn't?
qa.a: Truth can be said with care: naming a real strength, the high notes, and one clear thing to work on, which helped Lakshmi instead of crushing her.

qa.q: How did Sunaina's words affect Lakshmi?
qa.a: Lakshmi was hurt enough to drop out of the choir and stopped looking at Sunaina.

grounding: Shows a teenager who prides herself on blunt honesty realising her harsh verdict on a friend's singing served her own need to feel superior.
